solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: distractors A, B, C are each directly contradicted by the passage (A by para 2, B by para 5's 'may also matter for heat', C by para 5's 'its rivals have so far lacked'), so the item is easier than a typical main-idea item
minor: D says 'the most support', which slightly overstates the passage's hedged ending ('None of this proves...'), but it is clearly the best choice
R035-01.notes: Passage surveys explanations and concludes that only the fly hypothesis has controlled experimental support.

flags: minor: overlaps conceptually with R035-01; choice A here ('evidence that can distinguish among the explanations') previews the passage's structure and the main idea
R035-02.notes: The sentence sets up the rest of the passage, which describes tests that discriminate among hypotheses. B (disproved) and D (new explanation) are unsupported.

flags: minor: D (hear and smell prey) is a weak lure that borrows words from later in the paragraph; A and C are easy to rule out
R035-03.notes: The study treated the defenders' vision argument as worth testing and modeled predator visual acuity.

R035-04.notes: Within the range where stripes can be resolved, the lion would already have detected the zebra by other senses, so stripes add no concealment there; beyond it they blur to gray. A is extreme ('every'); B and D are unsupported.

flags: answer cue: A closely paraphrases the topic sentence of para 4 ('Correlation, though, could not show that the stripes did anything'), which makes the item mostly a lookup
minor: C and D contradict explicit text ('not with predators', 'a range of environmental factors'), so they are weak distractors
R035-05.notes: The analysis was correlational and could not show a causal effect on bites/landings.

flags: minor: the stem quotes only the circling detail, but the key also depends on the next sentence (fewer landings); this is acceptable since it is a contrast, but C ('no effect') is a plausible lure for students who read only the quoted phrase
R035-06.notes: Equal circling means stripes don't keep flies from finding zebras; the difference shows up at landing. A is the opposite trap.

flags: minor: the phrase 'not the horses themselves' is a little compressed; the idea is that the uncovered head serves as a within-animal control
R035-07.notes: Same horses and equal head landings across coats show that the coat pattern, not differences in the horses' attractiveness, reduced body landings. C overgeneralizes (heads were not protected); B and D are unsupported.

R035-08.notes: Each idea has had its supporters. A ('winners') is the common-meaning lure.

flags: minor: overlaps with R035-05; both test the role of the 2014 geographic correlation
minor: D undercuts only the correlational evidence, not the 2019 experiments, but it is still the only choice that bears against the fly hypothesis
R035-09.notes: Bold stripes concentrated where flies are rare would contradict the 2014 association. A bears on camouflage; B is compatible with multiple purposes; C is trivial because circling was never the measure that showed the effect.

passage_notes: Scientific claims match the published studies: Melin et al. 2016 (PLoS ONE) on predator acuity, with stripes resolvable within about 50 m in daylight and less at dusk; Caro et al. 2014 (Nature Communications) on the biogeography of equid striping; and Caro et al. 2019 (PLoS ONE), the farm in Britain with similar approach rates, fewer landings, and black/white/striped horse coats with equal head landings. No factual problems found. Minor note: the passage describes only one experimental program as 'experiments', which is fair. Some other evidence, such as the painted-cattle study, is omitted, but that does not affect any item.
